neu-acute-ischemic-stroke.title: Acute ischemic stroke
neu-acute-ischemic-stroke.blurb: Right facial droop, from occlusion of a cerebral artery with downstream infarction.
neu-acute-ischemic-stroke.summary: Acute ischemic stroke presents with abrupt right-sided weakness and slurred speech beginning 70 minutes ago, typically with right facial droop, dysarthria, and 3/5 strength in the right arm. Immediate noncontrast CT of the head confirms it, and thrombolytic evaluation against the treatment window is the initial management.

sections.heading: Overview
paras: The presentation that names acute ischemic stroke is abrupt right-sided weakness and slurred speech beginning 70 minutes ago; the process behind it is occlusion of a cerebral artery with downstream infarction. Sections below follow one conventional sequence — mechanism, presentation, confirmation, management — and each can be read on its own.

Prevalence estimates depend heavily on the setting in which they were gathered; referral series and community series describe different populations. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that the scan’s first job is to exclude hemorrhage; the clock’s job is everything else.

sections.heading: Mechanism
paras: At the centre of the problem is occlusion of a cerebral artery with downstream infarction. Tracing the picture back to that single process explains why the individual findings travel together rather than appearing in isolation.

Reserve within the affected system means measurable derangement often precedes anything the patient notices. Understanding this is what makes thrombolytic evaluation against the treatment window the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.

sections.heading: Clinical presentation
paras: Patients most often describe abrupt right-sided weakness and slurred speech beginning 70 minutes ago, and it is the tempo of that history — how quickly it arrived and whether it is progressing — that carries the diagnostic weight.

Presentations at the extremes of age are frequently less typical, and a normal early course does not exclude the diagnosis. A history of abrupt right-sided weakness and slurred speech beginning 70 minutes ago in the right context is enough to bring the diagnosis to the front of the differential.

sections.heading: Examination
paras: The sign to look for is right facial droop, dysarthria, and 3/5 strength in the right arm; it is more specific than the rest of the examination and is worth eliciting carefully.
Interobserver agreement for the classic signs is only moderate, which is a reason to weigh them alongside the history rather than above it.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paras: Immediate noncontrast CT of the head is the initial study, chosen because it confirms the diagnosis and separates it from the alternatives that present the same way.

A negative result is only as useful as the probability it was applied to, which is the argument for estimating that probability first. The alternative most often confused with it is guillain-Barré syndrome, which is compared below.
